The first name

Thursday, 7 May 2036, late in the evening, in Bertrand and Amina’s flat. The baby is due on Saturday. The third column of the “Nous” spreadsheet is still empty. Rose-Hélène has come to bring a book of first names.
Two days left, and the “First name” column is still empty. Whereas everything else has been ready for weeks.
You want a Senegalese name, while my mother would like a saint’s name. We’ll never get out of this.
Instead of arguing, look at my book. There are three thousand names in it.
Far from arguing, sweetheart, we’re negotiating. It’s very different.
Unlike your mother, Rose-Hélène, Amina negotiates with a spreadsheet program. I don’t stand a chance.
I was suggesting Odile if it’s a girl, and Henri if it’s a boy.
That’s very beautiful. On the other hand, it might mean a lot of Odiles and Henris in the network.
Generous as your suggestion is, it’s not very original. There are already four Odiles at the school in Corsica.
On the contrary! The more there are, the more we’re a family.
As much as I love tradition, I’d like this child to have a name of their own.
Then let’s leave the column empty until we see the baby’s face. Instead of choosing now.
(she sighs) You, who hate empty cells…
Not that one. That one is the most beautiful cell in the spreadsheet.

1. Alors que, tandis que + indicative
Both express a CONTRAST between two facts (“while”, “whereas”). Unlike concession (bien que), they are followed by the INDICATIVE:
Everything is ready, whereas the column is empty.
Don’t confuse: “bien que” + SUBJUNCTIVE (concession: “although”), but “alors que” + INDICATIVE (contrast: “whereas”). “Bien qu’il soit fatigué” ↔ “alors qu’il est fatigué”.
2. Au lieu de, loin de + infinitive
au lieu de + inf.
instead of (doing)
Au lieu de vous disputer, regardez mon livre.
au lieu de + noun
Il a pris du thé au lieu du café.
loin de + inf.
far from (on the contrary)
Loin de s’inquiéter, elle souriait.
sans + inf.
without (doing)
Il est parti sans rien dire.
“Loin de là !” = “Far from it!” — a very common expression in conversation.
3. Contrairement à, à l’inverse de
To compare two opposite people or things:
Contrary to what people think, he likes surprises.
Unlike his sister, he speaks little.
Watch the contraction: “contrairement AU médecin”, “contrairement AUX autres”.
4. En revanche, par contre, au contraire
standard, written
on the other hand (a different aspect)
informal, spoken
standard
on the contrary (denies what was said)
pourtant / cependant
It’s very beautiful. On the other hand, it isn’t original. (another aspect)
— Are you tired? — On the contrary, I’m in great shape! (contradicts)
In the DELF B2, in writing, prefer “en revanche” to “par contre”.
5. Contrastive “si” and “autant… autant”
“Si” can express contrast (not condition), with the indicative. “Autant… autant” weighs two attitudes against each other:
Generous as your suggestion is, it isn’t original. (si = although, granted that)
He may be shy, but he isn’t cold.

La case vide

On Saturday 9 May 2036, the due date, nothing happened. Absolutely nothing. Amina woke up at six as usual, checked the suitcase that had been ready by the door for a month, reread her spreadsheet, and waited. Bertrand hadn’t gone to bed. He had spent the night sitting in the living room, dressed, the car keys in his hand, while Amina slept peacefully.

It was the first time reality had refused to obey one of Amina’s spreadsheets. She took it far more calmly than everyone else. Instead of worrying, she baked a cake, tidied two cupboards and called her mother in Dakar to tell her not to change her ticket. Bertrand, on the contrary, called the maternity ward three times before noon to ask whether it was normal for a baby to be late.

The midwife who answered the third time had a calm, slightly amused voice. Her name was Mrs Leroy. She explained that babies, unlike trains, didn’t have timetables, and that most of them arrived late. Then she asked for the mother’s name. When Bertrand said “Amina Diallo-Vidal”, she fell silent for a moment. She asked whether it was the lady with the spreadsheets, the one from the waltz.

It was the same Mrs Leroy who had helped Henri-Ion into the world five years earlier, on a snowy night, at the same Croix-Rousse maternity hospital. She was sixty-three now, would retire in June, and remembered that night perfectly. She told Bertrand not to worry. She added that if the baby happened to arrive during her shift, she would look after the waltz family herself.

Throughout the pregnancy, Amina and Bertrand had been as different as could be. She had planned everything: the room, the pushchair, the vaccinations, the sleep schedule, in a two-hundred-and-forty-line spreadsheet. He, on the contrary, had planned nothing at all, except one thing. Every evening he read aloud to the baby, his hand on Amina’s belly. He read Court of Auditors reports. He said they were what sent it to sleep best.

Mariama had arrived from Dakar on 5 May, with a suitcase of baby clothes knitted by all the women in her family. She had settled into the little guest room and taken charge of the kitchen, the house and her son-in-law’s nerves. While Amina rested, Mariama taught Bertrand to make thiéboudienne. She said a man who could cook rice with fish was ready to become a father.

Bertrand had ruined the rice three times. The first time it was overcooked. The second, undercooked. The third, he had forgotten the fish, which Mariama had never seen in forty years of cooking. She had laughed for ten minutes. Then she had said it didn’t matter, and that fatherhood, unlike rice, wasn’t ruined by a mistake in the measurements. You just had to be there, and start again the next day.

On Sunday, to keep Bertrand busy, Mariama took them to the Parc de la Tête d’Or. Amina walked slowly on her mother’s arm, while Bertrand walked behind them, ready to step in at the slightest sign. They stopped in front of the big lime tree by the lake, the one Isabelle had kept a flower from in a book. Amina put her hand on the bark, as Rose-Hélène always did. She told the baby, under her breath, that it could come whenever it liked. There was no hurry.

Sunday went by, then Monday, then Tuesday. Still nothing. Amina carried on working from the sofa, on her computer, as if nothing were happening. She had finished the network’s accounts for the year, prepared the budget for the Dakar school and corrected two of Lamine’s spreadsheets. Bertrand wasn’t working at all any more. He had been on leave since 8 May, and spent his days watching his wife the way you watch a bomb.

On Tuesday a card arrived from Paris. It was signed Paul Delmas. The critic had heard the news from Léonie. He wrote that he had never had children, that he sometimes regretted it, and that he wished the baby its mother’s spreadsheets and its father’s patience. On the back of the card he had drawn three notes, clumsily, in biro. Amina said that for a man who hated sentimental films, it wasn’t bad at all.

On Wednesday evening, Amina announced that she would go to the Thursday orchestra rehearsal as usual. Bertrand protested. Mariama protested. Mrs Leroy, whom Amina had called for her opinion, said that as long as she felt well, nothing was stopping her, and that music had never harmed any baby. Bertrand pointed out that Bernard Delorme played the trumpet. Mrs Leroy said that, on the other hand, she couldn’t guarantee anything about that.

That evening Bertrand played the waltz on the violin, very softly, beside the bed, as he had done every evening since the sixth month. The baby always moved during the first two verses. Then, at the silence, it stopped. Every time. Amina had recorded the phenomenon twenty-seven times in a spreadsheet. She said this baby already knew the rule. Bertrand said it was a coincidence. He said it less and less loudly.

So on Thursday 14 May, at seven in the evening, Amina walked into the Salle Hélène Morel, forty-one weeks pregnant, with her little silver triangle in her pocket. The whole hall stood up to applaud her. Théo had set up a comfortable armchair for her in the front row, with cushions. The baker had brought croissants. The school caretaker had parked his car right outside the door, facing the street, just in case.

The rehearsal started normally. They were working on a new piece, a Romanian dance Sorina had sent from Bucharest. Then, at half past eight, Théo announced the waltz, as every Thursday. The orchestra played the first verse, then the second. Amina had taken out her triangle. At the third verse, everyone stopped for the silence. Eight bars. And in the middle of the silence, on the fifth bar, Amina gave a little cry.

It wasn’t the triangle. The triangle had fallen to the floor with a little silvery sound that rang through the whole hall. Amina had doubled over in her armchair, her hands on her belly. She looked up at Bertrand, in the second row of violins. She said, very calmly, despite the pain: “I think the column is about to be filled.” Then she added: “But finish the waltz first.”

Nobody finished the waltz. For the first time since the orchestra was founded, the silence of the third verse lasted much longer than eight bars, and it ended in complete chaos. Bertrand dropped his violin, which Isabelle caught just in time. The caretaker ran to get his car. Bernard Delorme played a fanfare on the trumpet without anyone knowing why. And Théo, instead of conducting, called the maternity ward.

Amina was the only one who kept calm. While everyone ran in all directions, she took out her phone and noted the time of the first contraction in a spreadsheet she had prepared for the purpose. Eight thirty-four. Then she asked Bertrand to fetch the suitcase. Bertrand replied that the suitcase was at home, by the door. Amina looked at him. For the first time in her life, she had forgotten something.

On the phone, the maternity ward told Théo they should come straight away, but there was no need to bring the whole orchestra. Théo passed the message on. Nobody listened. In five minutes the instruments were in their cases, the music stands folded, the lights off. The bus driver offered to take everyone in the line C bus, which was parked at the depot two streets away. Théo said that might not be a good idea.

The school caretaker drove them to the maternity hospital in twelve minutes, which was a record, with Mariama in the front seat and Bertrand in the back, holding Amina’s hand and repeating things that made no sense at all. Rose-Hélène, who had come to the rehearsal with her father, wanted to go too. Julien stopped her. So she ran with Isabelle to the rue d’Austerlitz, two streets away, to fetch the suitcase.

In the car, Mariama was singing. She sang in Wolof, in a low, steady voice, a song nobody else knew. The school caretaker drove through amber lights, apologising each time. Bertrand counted the seconds between contractions out loud, getting it wrong. Amina, between two contractions, corrected his sums. At the third red light she said that if anyone in this car had to keep a cool head, it was clearly going to be her.

But the suitcase wasn’t in the rue d’Austerlitz. It was at Amina and Bertrand’s, in the Croix-Rousse, on the other side of the hill. Rose-Hélène realised this when she arrived, breathless, in front of her own door. Isabelle laughed in spite of everything. They took a taxi. The driver asked where they were going. Rose-Hélène answered: “To fetch a suitcase, then to the maternity hospital, and quickly, please, because a column is being filled.”

At Amina’s, the downstairs neighbour let them in with the spare keys. Rose-Hélène found the suitcase straight away, by the door, with a label on which Amina had written: “Maternity suitcase — do not forget”. Rose-Hélène found that very funny. On the way, she glanced into the baby’s room. The walls were painted pale green. And on the wall above the cot, Bertrand had painted three musical notes by hand.

At the maternity hospital, Mrs Leroy was waiting for them at the entrance. She had seen Théo’s call and had swapped her shift with a colleague so as to be there. She took charge of Amina with a gentleness Bertrand would never forget. Unlike him, she didn’t run, didn’t shout, didn’t repeat meaningless sentences. She spoke slowly, the way you speak to someone you love. Bertrand said later that she had reminded him of Odile.

The night was long. Much longer than expected. Amina recorded every contraction in her spreadsheet until midnight, then handed the phone to Bertrand and told him to carry on. Bertrand carried on until one in the morning, then forgot. Mrs Leroy told him kindly that spreadsheets were all very well, but tonight his wife mostly needed his hand. Bertrand put the phone away. He didn’t let go of Amina’s hand again.

Around eleven, Mrs Leroy asked Bertrand to step out for ten minutes while she did an examination. Bertrand found himself alone in the corridor, under a white light, in front of a broken coffee machine. He thought of his father. He didn’t know why. His father, who had never told him he loved him, and whom he had never really forgiven for the violin. He wondered what kind of father he would be. He found no answer. The door opened again.

In the waiting room on the ground floor, more and more people were gathering. Mariama first, praying in silence, prayer beads in her hand. Then Rose-Hélène and Isabelle with the suitcase, arriving at ten. Then Julien and Ioana. Then Théo, Bernard Delorme and his trumpet, the baker and his croissants, the bus driver, and Nadia, Inès’s mother, who was working the night shift at the hospital next door and dropped by every hour with news.

Inès and Sami arrived around eleven, running, still in evening clothes: they had just come from a concert. Nadia, Inès’s mother, came down to give them news. Everything was fine, she said, but it would be a while yet. She added that first babies always took their time, unlike second ones, which often arrived in the car. Bernard Delorme asked whether they could know more. Nadia said no, and that he’d do better to get some sleep.

At midnight a nurse came to ask, politely but firmly, whether all these people were really family. Mariama looked round the room, then at the nurse. She answered yes. All of them. The nurse asked how that was possible, with such different faces. Mariama said they didn’t share the same blood, but they shared the same waltz, and in her family that counted just as much. The nurse hesitated. Then she brought extra chairs.

To pass the time, Julien told the story of the night Henri-Ion was born, in this same maternity hospital, five years earlier. The snow, the empty streets, the taxi that didn’t come. Ioana singing in Romanian. The midwife, already Mrs Leroy, who had agreed to let Odile and Isabelle approve the name by phone at three in the morning. Ioana said she mostly remembered one thing: Julien had fainted in the corridor. Julien denied it. Everyone half believed him.

By two in the morning, most of them had fallen asleep on their chairs. Bernard Delorme was snoring softly, his trumpet on his knees. The baker had gone to make his bread, promising to come back with brioches. Rose-Hélène was asleep on Isabelle’s shoulder, the harmonica in her hand. Only Mariama wasn’t asleep. She was watching the lift door and singing very quietly, in Wolof, a lullaby her own mother used to sing to her in Dakar.

Around three, in the room, came the hardest moment. Amina, who had been so calm all night, said for the first time that she couldn’t do it. Bertrand didn’t know what to do. So he did the only thing he knew how to do. He hummed the waltz, very softly, in her ear, slowly, off-key. Amina closed her eyes. Mrs Leroy was counting. And at the third verse, Bertrand fell silent. Amina breathed. Eight bars.

The baby was born on Friday 15 May 2036, at twelve minutes past four in the morning, while everyone in the waiting room was asleep. It was a little girl. She weighed three kilos one hundred, measured forty-nine centimetres, and had black, curly hair like her mother. She cried very loudly, once, then suddenly fell silent when Mrs Leroy laid her on Amina’s chest. As if she had understood that there had to be silence.

Bertrand looked at his daughter. He said nothing. He could no longer speak. He, who hadn’t cried since his father’s funeral thirty years earlier, was crying like a child. Amina was smiling. Far from being exhausted, she looked more awake than ever. She was looking at her daughter with extreme attention, as if checking a spreadsheet line by line. After a long moment she said: “Everything is correct. Nothing is missing.”

Mrs Leroy asked for the name, for the wristband. Amina and Bertrand looked at each other. They still hadn’t decided anything. They had said they would wait to see her face. Now they could see it. A small round face, eyes closed, with Bertrand’s mouth and Mariama’s eyebrows. Amina said it was Bertrand’s turn to choose. Bertrand said it was hers. Mrs Leroy said she had time, she would come back in an hour.

Before leaving the room, Mrs Leroy told them a secret. In forty years of practice she had helped three thousand one hundred and twelve babies into the world. She had written down every name in a little blue notebook, starting with the first, in 1996. She had never shown the notebook to anyone. She said with a smile that she too, in her own way, kept spreadsheets. Amina asked whether she could see it one day. Mrs Leroy said yes, but only once the cell was filled.

During that hour, hardly a word was spoken in the room. Bertrand held his daughter in his arms for the first time, with the same clumsiness and the same care with which he used to hold Gérard Thiébaut’s violin. He was afraid of breaking her. Amina watched him. And suddenly the little one opened her eyes. Big, dark, very serious eyes, which looked at Bertrand as if they already knew him. Bertrand murmured a name.

He said “Awa”. Amina looked up. Awa was the name of her grandmother, Mariama’s mother, who had died in Dakar when Amina was seven. The one who sang the lullaby in Wolof. Amina had never talked to Bertrand about her, or almost never — just once, years before. He had remembered. She asked why that name. Bertrand said he didn’t know. He had looked at her, and it had just come.

Then Bertrand added something Amina didn’t know. Awa, in Wolof, was also the form of the name Eve. The first name in the Bible. His own mother, who absolutely wanted a saint’s name, couldn’t say a thing. And at the same time it was a Senegalese name, a name from Amina’s family. And at the same time again, nobody else in the class would have it. He had checked everything. Amina burst out laughing despite her exhaustion.

She asked him how long he had known all this. Bertrand admitted he had been researching for three months, in secret, in the evenings after rehearsals. He had studied the meaning of four hundred names in six languages. He had written it all down. Amina asked where. Bertrand took out his phone, a little embarrassed. He had made a spreadsheet. The first spreadsheet of his life. It was called “Her”. It had four hundred and twelve lines.

Amina looked at the spreadsheet for a long time. She said it was badly built, the columns weren’t aligned, formulas were missing, and she had never seen anything so beautiful. Then she took her own phone, opened the “Nous” file and handed it to Bertrand. She said it was up to him to fill in the cell. Bertrand hesitated. Then he wrote, slowly, one letter after another: “Awa”.

He added a second name, after looking at Amina, who nodded. “Awa Odile”. The first for the grandmother in Dakar, the second for the old lady on the landing. Two women who had never met, who didn’t speak the same language, and who had both sung for children who weren’t their own. Mrs Leroy came back at that moment. She wrote the name on the little wristband. She said it was very pretty.

At half past five, Bertrand went down to the waiting room. He hadn’t slept for two days, his shirt was crumpled, his grey hair a mess, and he had the widest smile anyone had ever seen on him. Half the room was still asleep. He didn’t know how to announce the news without waking everyone at once. So he did the only thing that came to mind. He whistled three notes.

Rose-Hélène woke up first. She opened her eyes, saw Bertrand, saw his smile, and understood. She answered on the harmonica, the next three notes, half asleep. Then Mariama answered by singing. Then all the others woke up, one after another, and answered in their turn, whistling, singing, or, in Bernard Delorme’s case, playing the trumpet in a hospital waiting room at half past five in the morning.

The night nurse came running. She was about to get angry, then she saw the faces. She asked whether it was a girl or a boy. Bertrand said: “A girl. Awa Odile. Three kilos one hundred.” The nurse smiled. She said that this time she hadn’t heard a thing, but it absolutely mustn’t happen again, because the trumpet, on the other hand, had woken the whole paediatric ward. Bernard Delorme apologised. He looked only half guilty.

Mariama was the first to go up and see her granddaughter. She stood for a long time in front of the transparent cot without a word. Then she took the baby in her arms, with movements that thirty years of school and forty years of life hadn’t erased. When Amina told her the name, Mariama closed her eyes. She murmured something in Wolof. Amina translated for Bertrand: “My mother has come back. She just took another road.”

That morning, Mariama thought of the little girl she had been in 1978, on quay number four, with her mess tin, listening to a sailor play the harmonica. She was ten. She didn’t know that music would follow her all her life, to Lyon, to this hospital room, to this granddaughter asleep in her arms. She told herself that life was stranger than any novel. And much more patient.

Then Mariama sang the lullaby. The same one her mother used to sing to her, the same one she had sung to Amina and Moussa, the same one she had been singing softly in the waiting room. Awa fell asleep at the second verse. Bertrand asked what the words said. Mariama said it was hard to translate. But roughly, the song said the night was long, the sea was big, and there would always be someone on the quay.

Around seven, the baker came back as promised. He had made a special brioche, triangle-shaped, with three musical notes drawn in icing sugar. He put it on the waiting-room table without a word, then left to open his bakery. Bernard Delorme, woken by the smell, said it was the best brioche he had ever eaten. He ate half of it before anyone thought of keeping some for the parents.

During the morning, messages arrived from everywhere. Moussa, from Dakar, with a photo of his three children holding a sign saying “Welcome Awa”. Lamine, with a kora recording. Sorina and Andrei, from Bucharest, with a video of Viorica playing the three notes on the piano and saying that at her age every birth was good news for her personally. Grandma, from Iași, asking whether anyone had thought of putting a red bracelet on her against the evil eye.

Yves Le Goff phoned himself, from Brittany, in his old sailor’s voice, weaker than before but as clear as ever. He was ninety-two. He told Bertrand he had known storms, shipwrecks and ports all over the world, but there was nothing more terrifying on earth than holding your first child. Bertrand said that was exactly it. Yves laughed. He said: “Then you’re a real sailor now.”

Henri-Ion went up first, with Ioana, late in the morning. He looked at Awa through the side of the cot for a very long time, his nose pressed against the plastic. Then he asked three questions. Why she was so small. Whether she spoke French or Wolof. And whether she could already whistle. Amina answered all three. Henri-Ion thought about it. Then he announced that since nobody was teaching her Romanian, he would do it himself. He started straight away: “Bună, Awa.”

In the afternoon Rose-Hélène was allowed to go up. She had put on her best dress and was holding a parcel wrapped in newspaper. She tiptoed up to the cot. Awa was asleep. Rose-Hélène looked at her for a long time, very seriously. Then she said she was smaller than expected, but much prettier than in the spreadsheet. Amina asked which spreadsheet. Rose-Hélène said she had made one too.

In the parcel was a harmonica. A tiny child’s harmonica in red plastic, which Rose-Hélène had bought with her savings, two euros a week for two months. She laid it in the cot next to Awa, very gently. She said Awa wouldn’t be able to play it straight away, obviously. But at least she would know there was someone on the other side. She added that she would come and teach her the three notes as soon as she had teeth.

Bertrand pointed out that you didn’t need teeth to play the harmonica. Rose-Hélène thought about it. She said that in that case she would start next week. Then she took out her own harmonica, Henri’s, and played the three notes very softly over the cot. Awa opened her eyes. She didn’t cry. She looked at Rose-Hélène with her big serious eyes for exactly eight seconds. Then she went back to sleep.

Isabelle came later, alone, with a small parcel wrapped in tissue paper. It was a baby blanket of white wool, slightly yellowed, knitted by hand. Odile had knitted it in 1974, for Isabelle’s birth. Isabelle had kept it for fifty-two years in a wardrobe, without knowing who it was for. She laid it over Awa. She said that now she knew. Amina cried for the first time since the birth. She said it was tiredness. Nobody believed her.

Bertrand’s mother arrived the next day by train from Clermont-Ferrand. Her name was Geneviève; she was eighty-one, had been a widow for thirty years and was very devout. She had always been a little afraid of Amina, her spreadsheets and her very large family. She wanted a saint’s name. When Bertrand told her “Awa”, she went pale. Then he explained that it was Eve, in Wolof. Geneviève thought for a long moment.

Then she said that Eve wasn’t exactly a saint, but she was everyone’s mother, which was no doubt worth more. She took Awa in her arms. She looked at her curly hair, her dark eyes, her mouth that looked like her son’s. She said under her breath that her husband would have been proud. Then she took a small parcel out of her bag. It was Bertrand’s old violin, the one his father had sold.

Bertrand couldn’t believe his eyes. His mother explained that his father had never sold it. He had lied. He had hidden the violin in the attic in 1996, because he wanted his son to study something serious instead of becoming a musician. He had regretted that lie all his life without ever daring to admit it. Before he died, he had asked his wife to give the violin back to Bertrand on the day he had a child. She had waited thirty years.

It was a small three-quarter student violin, its varnish worn, with a broken string. Bertrand held it for a long time without a word, next to the cot. Then he said this violin wouldn’t be for him. He would have it repaired in Mirecourt by Gérard Thiébaut. And he would keep it for Awa. If she ever wanted to play one day, she would have her grandfather’s violin. If not, never mind. It would stay on the wall above her bed, like a question.

They went home on Monday. Bertrand drove at twenty kilometres an hour the whole way, both hands on the wheel, glancing in the rear-view mirror every ten seconds. Behind them a bus honked. It was the line C driver, who had recognised them and was honking to congratulate them. Bertrand thought he had made a driving mistake. He pulled over to check. Amina was laughing so hard she woke Awa.

The following Thursday, Amina and Bertrand came to rehearsal with Awa, who was six days old. She was asleep in a baby carrier against her father’s chest. Théo asked the orchestra to play very softly. Everyone played very softly except Bernard Delorme, who played as usual, that is, very loudly. Awa didn’t stir. She slept through the Romanian dance, the first two verses of the waltz, and the trumpet.

Then came the third verse. The orchestra fell silent. Eight bars. And in the silence, though she had slept through all the noise, Awa woke up. She opened her big serious eyes and looked around her, as if someone had called her. She didn’t cry. She waited. On the fifth bar, Amina struck her little silver triangle once — the one that had fallen to the floor a week earlier. Awa smiled.

Léonie Garnier was in the hall that evening, with her triangle but without her camera. She had promised Julien not to film anything else without permission. She regretted her promise for exactly eight bars. Then she took out her notebook and wrote a single sentence, which she later showed Amina: “Some things are more beautiful when nobody films them.” Amina said that for a director it was a very brave sentence.

Mrs Leroy said later that it was impossible, that a six-day-old baby couldn’t smile, that it was a reflex. Bertrand said he knew. Amina said it was recorded anyway, in the spreadsheet, on the line “First smile”. That evening, when they got home, she opened the “Nous” file and added a column. A new empty cell. She headed it “First word”. Bertrand asked whether they would have to wait long again. Amina said yes. And that was exactly what made it so beautiful.

Reading: First names — tradition or originality?
An article from a parenting magazine. Notice how the author contrasts the two camps. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Prénoms : tradition ou originalité ?
Choosing a first name has never been so difficult. Whereas our grandparents often took the name of a saint or an ancestor, today’s parents are spoilt for choice.
On one side are the supporters of tradition. For them, a name links the child to its family and its history. Far from being old-fashioned, an old name is said to be a form of memory.
On the other side are those who seek originality. Unlike their elders, they want a unique name that nobody else in the class has. Instead of looking to the past, they look to the future.
Mixed families often experience this dilemma more intensely. While one parent wishes to honour one culture, the other thinks of another language, of other grandparents.
Complicated as this choice may seem, it is also an opportunity. A name that can be pronounced just as well in French as in Wolof or Romanian is, on the contrary, a bridge between two worlds.

A Lyon midwife told us her secret: “As much as parents hesitate for nine months, they often know immediately, as soon as they see the baby’s face.” On the other hand, she wouldn’t say how many times she had been wrong.
